newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Businessman accuses ex-Yeltsin aide of blackmail.
newsitem.headline: Businessman accuses ex-Yeltsin aide of blackmail.

text.p: A businessman who narrowly escaped assassination in June appeared on television on Sunday to repeat allegations of blackmail against a former top aide of Russian President Boris Yeltsin.

Boris Fyodorov, the former head of the National Sports Foundation, told NTV television that Yeltsin's former chief bodyguard, General Alexander Korzhakov, and his deputy tried to force him to pay $40 million.
Yeltsin sacked Korzhakov, his long time confidant, and several other top officials shortly after the first round of the presidential election in June.

Fyodorov said he had been summoned to Korzhakov's Kremlin office where the then powerful Yeltsin aide demanded a share of alleged illegal gains made by the foundation, which enjoyed import privileges to help raise funds for sports.
"They told me: 'You have stolen so much, now it's time to share'," he told a popular weekly programme, Itogi.
Fyodorov first accused Korzhakov of blackmail in a newspaper article soon after the assassination attempt. Korzhakov denied the accusation.
The prosecutor's office has started an investigation into Fyodorov's allegation but no results have been made public so far.
Korzhakov was not immediately available for comment on the renewed allegations.
Fyodorov said that after he refused to pay, Korzhakov ordered the chief of border guards not to let him out of the country.
Fyodorov said Shamil Tarpishchev, Yeltsin's tennis coach, had also made similar demands.

ORT state television reported on Saturday that Yeltsin had sacked Tarpishchev from two powerful posts in the Kremlin sports administration -- chairman of the State Committee on Sports and Tourism and chairman of the Presidential Coordinating Committee on Sports and Tourism.
Fyodorov said two attackers stabbed him 12 times in June near his apartment bloc in a posh Moscow residential area.
"The guys looked quite cool trying to kill me," he said. "They did not seem to be in a hurry which is strange in a compound full of police. It looked like they had noone to fear."
Earlier in the year Fyodorov was detained for several days by police on suspicion that he was involved in drug sales.
